title: HashX PoW kernel compiled for sm_75 (Tesla T4): interpreter vs compiled program
how: Kaggle notebook on a Tesla T4 (40 SMs, 1590 MHz, CUDA 13.0.88), built and run by src/sass/kaggle_t4_hashx.py
correctness: all three variants reproduce the repo's own HashX vector (beyond/vectors/hx_vectors.hex case 0, nonce 0) exactly

measured.shape: 8,388,608 nonces x 3 reps, one 512-instruction program per hash

what_was_found: the shipped kernel indexes r[0..7] with runtime dst/src values, so the register file lives in LOCAL MEMORY: 20 LDL + 19 STL per hash, plus an LDG for every instruction fetch out of the global program array

variant 2 pins the register file with a uniform switch and moves the program to __constant__: 1.39x at ILP 1, but MORE ILP destroys it (0.82x at 2, 0.36x at 4) because 8 x 64-bit registers per lane plus the SipRound state does not fit and it spills

variant 3 removes the interpreter entirely: the program is fixed for a whole challenge, so it is emitted as 512 straight-line statements with constant register names, one label for the program's single taken branch, and no program memory at all. 19.9-22.4x over the shipped kernel
why_the_jit_is_the_real_answer: an interpreter charges one constant fetch, one 11-way dispatch and two local-memory accesses per VM instruction; the arithmetic itself is one 64-bit op. At 512 instructions that overhead is about 20x the useful work, which is exactly the measured ratio
caveat: the JIT kernel is per-challenge code, the same thing a real deployment does host-side when it exports the program. It was generated here from case 0 of the repo's vector file; a production backend would generate it from hashx_export at challenge time
negative_result: ILP does not help HashX either, in both variants, for opposite reasons: the interpreter variant spills the register file, and the JIT variant is already issue-bound with 48 registers
